lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you learned to disagree well. What should you criticise in an argument, the idea or the person? (The idea.) Today: hard choices, called dilemmas, and how to reason about them.

A dilemma is a choice where every option has something good and something bad about it. There may be no perfect answer, but some answers have better reasons than others. Thinking carefully about right and wrong is called ethics.

Three ways to think it through. First, consequences: which choice leads to the most good and the least harm for everyone affected? The thinkers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that we should aim for the greatest happiness.

Second, fairness: does the choice treat people equally, keep promises and respect their rights? Would it be fair if everyone did it? Immanuel Kant argued that some things, such as telling the truth, are right whatever the results.

Third, kindness, or care: who might be hurt or left out, and how can we look after them? Many faiths and traditions teach a golden rule: treat others as you would like to be treated. Good choices often use all three ways at once.

Worked dilemma: Mimi sees a friend copy homework. Consequences: copying hurts the friend's learning. Fairness: others did their own work. Kindness: talk to the friend first and offer help. But if anyone could be in danger, always tell a trusted grown-up.

People who reason well can still disagree. Listen, say back what you heard, give your reasons, and be open to changing your mind, as you practised in grade 6. Respect the person, even when you disagree with the idea.

messages: The land should go to Ben.
So you think Ben was there first?
I see. I think sharing is fairer, because...

lesson.text: Try it in the world: discuss a server dilemma with friends: someone built on land others wanted. What is fair? What will happen? What is kind? Agree a rule and write your reasons on a sign. Next: in grade 8, democracies compared.

choices: a choice where each option has good and bad
exercises.explain: A choice where every option has something good and something bad about it.

choices: What will happen if we do it?
exercises.explain: “What will happen if we do it?” asks about results: consequences.

exercises.prompt: The golden rule says: treat others as you would like to be treated.
exercises.explain: True: many faiths and traditions teach it.

exercises.prompt: If a friend might be in danger, what should you do?
exercises.explain: Tell a trusted grown-up, even if you promised to keep a secret.

exercises.prompt: When you disagree with someone, what should you respect?
exercises.hint: Grade 6 taught you to criticise the idea. Who holds that idea, and how should they be treated?
exercises.explain: The person: disagree with the idea, respectfully.

items: Everyone should get the same chance.
More people will be helped this way.
He feels left out, so let's include him.
The rule must be the same for all.
A lie now could cause trouble later.
exercises.hint: Fairness: equal treatment. Consequences: what happens. Kindness: feelings and care.
exercises.explain: Fairness: same chance, same rule. Consequences: more helped, trouble later. Kindness: left out, her feelings.

exercises.prompt: Match each thinker or idea to its view.
exercises.hint: One counts results, one keeps duties, one is a rule of thumb, one is about looking after people.
exercises.explain: Bentham: the most happiness. Kant: duty whatever the results. Golden rule: treat others as you'd like. Care: look after people.

exercises.hint: Fairness is about treating people equally.
choices: everyone should get the same chance
it will make more people happy
exercises.explain: “Everyone should get the same chance” is about treating people equally: fairness.

exercises.prompt: Plan A helps 30 people and harms none; plan B helps 22 and harms none. Thinking only of consequences, how many more people does plan A help?
exercises.hint: Take the smaller number from the bigger.

exercises.prompt: People who reason well always agree.
exercises.hint: Can two careful thinkers weigh things differently?
exercises.explain: False: good reasoners can disagree; they listen and respect each other.

exercises.prompt: Bram promised to keep a secret, but his friend might be in danger. What comes first?
exercises.hint: Which matters more: a promise, or someone's safety?
exercises.explain: Keeping his friend safe: he should tell a trusted grown-up.

exercises.prompt: Zara finds a purse with a name in it. Which choice is fair, kind and ends well?
exercises.hint: Think of consequences, fairness and kindness together.
exercises.explain: Returning it is fair (it is theirs), kind (they will be relieved) and ends well for everyone.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a good discussion in order.
exercises.hint: You need to understand before you reply.
items: change your mind if theirs are better
exercises.explain: Listen, say back, give reasons, and be open to changing your mind.

exercises.prompt: Zara finds 50 gold on the path with no name. What is the most thoughtful choice?
exercises.hint: Someone may be looking for it.
choices: hand it in so the owner can claim it
exercises.explain: Handing it in lets the owner claim it: fair and kind.

exercises.prompt: A dilemma always has one perfect answer.
exercises.hint: What makes a choice a dilemma?
exercises.explain: False: every option has good and bad sides; we look for the best-reasoned answer.

exercises.prompt: Mimi's friend copied homework. Match each of Mimi's thoughts to the way of thinking it uses.
items: I'll talk to her first and help.
Treat her as you'd like to be.
exercises.hint: Results, equal treatment, looking after someone, or treating others as you would like?
exercises.explain: Hurting her learning is a consequence. Others doing their own work is about fairness. Talking first and helping is kindness, or care. Treating her as you would like to be treated is the golden rule.
